title: Dozens of greyhounds to land in Australia as NZ racing ban begins
content:
Charter flights to bring about 150 greyhounds to Australia as NZ racing ban begins
Sat 1 Aug 2026 at 2:48pm
In short:
A ban on greyhound racing came into effect in New Zealand today.
Greyhound Racing New Zealand has organised charter flights to export about 150 dogs to Australia for trainers to continue racing.
What's next?
It is estimated 1,400 greyhounds will retire from the sport and be rehomed in New Zealand.
Chartered flights will ferry up to 150 greyhounds to Australia as trainers pivot from a racing ban coming into effect in New Zealand.
The ban, which was first announced in December 2024 and legislated in April this year, took effect on Saturday after years of animal welfare concerns.
Ten greyhounds were euthanised during New Zealand's final racing season, including one days before the ban began.
Heather Simpson, the Greyhound Transition Agency (GTA) head, said she was aware that Greyhound Racing New Zealand had organised charter flights for about 150 dogs to go to Australia to continue racing.
"There is nothing in the legislation that stops trainers choosing to export their dogs to Australia; some of these dogs actually will be partly owned by Australians," she told Radio New Zealand.
Greyhound racing remains legal in most Australian jurisdictions, banned only in the Australian Capital Territory.
Plans for an industry phase-out in Tasmania have stalled after the government pulled a bill from the upper house in April when it appeared not to have enough support to pass.
Word of the chartered flights first emerged through a leaked message from a private greyhound racing group, Greens senator Mehreen Faruqi told a Senate Rural and Regional Affairs and Transport Legislation Committee hearing in April.
She said the move appeared "to be kind of a deliberate attempt to avoid" New Zealand's transition agency.
"If they survive, they will become the responsibility of Australians to rehome," she said.
"And you would know we're already in a rehoming crisis."
Brant Smith, a senior biosecurity executive at the Department of Agriculture and Fisheries, told the senate hearing the government had been working with New Zealand's Ministry for Primary Industries on the dogs' import.
He said they would be classed as "companion animals", but may be used for racing once in the country.
"As to how they are then used, that's not something that we have control over thereafter because they're being imported as companion animals like other animals … and this is not unusual," he said.
Mr Smith said a similar contingent of greyhounds was imported to Australia in April 2025.
"In the previous consignment, I think approximately 80 came similarly, and they were just imported under our normal conditions," he said.
It is estimated a further 1,400 dogs will remain in New Zealand and require rehoming by the GTA.
Ms Simpson said the rehomed dogs would be regularly checked under a welfare program.

title: Hong Kong mulls AI facial recognition-enabled drones to police smoking ban at construction sites, 39 fines issued so far
content:
Authorities have issued 39 fines since a smoking ban at construction sites came into effect last month, with the Labour Department saying it is looking into equipping drones with facial recognition tools to better enforce the new law.
Wan Chi-ping, the Labour Department’s assistant commissioner of occupational safety, said authorities have inspected nearly 1,400 construction sites since the smoking ban was introduced in mid-July.
Local media reported on Wednesday that a total of 39 fines had been issued, and authorities had also handed out 11 “improvement notices” at construction sites where anti-smoking measures were not up to standard.
Wan said the department has been using drones with cameras that have infrared sensors to help identify smoking on construction sites. The drones work by detecting higher temperatures to pinpoint potential instances of smoking, he added.
“We can adjust the thermal sensitivity threshold to 60 to 80°C, which is typically the temperature range for smoking. If a temperature of this range [is detected], a red dot will appear on the monitor,” Wan said in Cantonese.
But he added that none of the fines issued so far resulted from drone detection.
AI facial recognition-enabled drones
Wan said authorities are also looking into integrating artificial intelligence (AI) facial recognition tools into the drones. Research into adding such tools may take nine months to a year, he said.
The smoking ban is among a number of measures that the government proposed in the wake of the deadly Tai Po fire last November, which killed 168 people and displaced thousands in one of the worst blazes in Hong Kong history.
Authorities previously said that the blaze was most likely caused by smoking, citing the findings of a cross-departmental investigation.
The new rule designates all types of construction sites – including those for building repair, maintenance or renovation – as no smoking areas. Offenders face a fixed fine of HK$3,000.
Contractors responsible for construction works are required to ensure that no one smokes on their sites, with those failing to do so facing a maximum fine of HK$400,000.

why_adverse:
Two independent failures, either one sufficient.

FIRST: it does not exist yet. The Labour Department estimates nine months to a year of research to integrate facial recognition into the drones, and no fine has been issued on drone evidence. Solutions is for initiatives that WORK. solution_concreteness (6.56) is the top dimension and it fired on a proposal: every concrete detail in the article — 1,400 sites inspected, 39 fines, 11 improvement notices, HK$3,000 and HK$400,000 penalties, a 60-80°C thermal threshold — belongs to the smoking ban already in force, not to the AI system being scored. The lens read an enacted policy's enforcement statistics as evidence for an unbuilt system described in the same article. This is a general trap worth generalising from: an article about a proposed extension to a working programme carries the working programme's evidence.

SECOND: the mechanism is the objection. The intervention is facial-recognition drones surveilling construction workers. Nothing in the rubric prices what an intervention costs the people it is applied to. equity_access (4.50) asks who benefits from a solution, not who is subjected to it, and there is no dimension between them. community_practice_strength (1.20) is correctly near-zero and correctly carries almost no weight.

Scope this row carefully. The underlying smoking ban is a defensible response to the Tai Po fire that killed 168 people, and a fix that learns "workplace safety enforcement is adverse" is worse than the bug. The adverse signal is specifically biometric surveillance as the enforcement mechanism, scored above p99 before it exists.
misleading_features: Enforcement statistics from the already-live ban (1,400 sites inspected, 39 fines, 11 improvement notices) read as evidence the AI-drone system works; it has issued zero fines and is 9-12 months from existing
Numeric specificity as a proxy for concreteness — HK$3,000 / HK$400,000 penalties and a 60-80°C thermal detection range make an unbuilt system read as engineered
A named government department with a stated delivery timeline reads as a governance intervention in force (governance_intervention_strength 5.25) rather than an announced intention
A high-casualty precipitating event (168 deaths in the Tai Po fire) supplies stakes that lift systemic_impact (5.19) without any part of the intervention being realised
No dimension prices the intervention's cost to its subjects: facial recognition applied to workers is invisible to the rubric, since equity_access scores who benefits and not who is surveilled
